newsitem.title: JAPAN: New Japan-U.S. defence plan set to roil politics.
newsitem.headline: New Japan-U.S. defence plan set to roil politics.

text.p: Japan's ruling parties staked out cautious positions on new plans to beef up Japan-U.S. security ties on Monday, while the main opposition group seized on the proposals as a chance to shake up the coalition government.

The main parties' vagueness and jockeying raised concerns that debate on the vital issue of national security could take a back seat to short-term political concerns, leaving Japan unprepared to meet U.S. expectations embodied in the plans.

Proposals on Japan-U.S. military cooperation -- calling for use of Japanese airfields by U.S. warplanes in a conflict, Japanese involvement in minesweeping, enhanced intelligence gathering by Tokyo and Japan peacekeeping duties -- also expose political fault lines over the country's pacifist constitution.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto is a strong supporter of the new arrangements, which were revealed in an interim report on Saturday, and his leadership will be critical in implementing the plans.
However, the prime minister hedged on the meaning of Japan's new commitments, in case the issue roil ties between his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its coalition partners.
"Since it's an interim report, I suppose opinions differ (between Japan and the United States)," he said, noting that the final report is not due until November.
Hashimoto's remarks were designed not to ruffle Japanese public opinion and his coalition allies the Socialist Party, both of which are wary about an increased military role for Japan.

Parliament is set to adjourn next week until September at the earliest and is unlikely to discuss legislation to underpin any expanded bilateral security cooperation until the 1998 session begins early next year.
The new security arrangements would give Tokyo its highest military profile since World War Two.

Meanwhile, a long-brewing power rivalry within the LDP between those who favour keeping the three-year-old alliance of the LDP, the Socialists and the tiny Sakigake Party and those who want to dump those parties will intensify, analysts say.

In parliamentary elections last October, the LDP came up a dozen seats short of a simple majority in the 500-seat lower house, forming a government in an informal alliance with the Socialists and Sakigake.
LDP Secretary General Koichi Kato, a proponent of the three-party alliance, was optimistic that persuasion could keep the Socialists in the fold.
"We will be able to reach an understanding if we undertake thorough discussions among the three parties," Kato said.
Kato's rivals in the LDP, however, say the party should cut the Socialists loose and ally with the conservative Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), with which it has more in common.
"Without discussions with Shinshinto, we cannot work out the guidelines and legislation needed to prepare for emergencies," said Construction Minister Shizuka Kamei, an LDP stalwart.

In a test run of that alliance, the LDP and Shinshinto in April passed a special bill to forcibly renew government leases on land occupied by U.S. military bases, overcoming local landowners' opposition. The Socialists voted against the bill.

Shinshinto's initial response to the security pact guidelines suggest it will not simply join hands with the LDP without first trying to split up the ruling coalition -- if not the LDP itself -- over calls for opening debate on the constitution.
"We regret the fact that there has been no proper debate on the constitution," the party said in a statement.

Not only the Socialists but a sizable dovish faction in the LDP oppose opening debate on revising Japan's post-World War Two pacifist constitution, which confines its self-defence forces or military to protecting only Japanese territory.
